speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising under the provisions of Standing Order 31 with regard to an article that has appeared across the country. The article reports me as saying things that are anti-French and anti-Quebec.
The quotes that were used were taken from an article in Montreal's The Gazette written earlier this month in which I was discussing how my attitude has completely changed from that of when I was living in Montreal in 1978. I spoke of how I supported fostering better relations between the French and the English and how I myself am taking lessons in French. This, however, was omitted from the wire service story.

I want to apologize to those people who read the article and possibly got the impression that I was antiFrench and anti-Quebec. I am myself a member of an ethnic minority, and I can assure you I harbour no discriminatory feelings.

I believe that in Canada, being the cultural mosaic that it is, linguistic tolerance is one of the cornerstones of a Canadian democracy.

Mr. Speaker, the VIA Rail document recently presented
to the priorities and planning committee of cabinet and leaked by The Winnipeg Free Press shows this government's blatant disregard and short-sightedness toward tourism, one of Canada's leading industries.
The government spends millions of dollars promoting train travel as part of its tourism product, while it simultaneously does a hatchet job on VIA. The Vancouv-er-Montreal route which is to be scrapped completely is an internationally renowned favourite with foreign travellers and enjoys an annual booking of over half a million passengers.
Cutting VIA routes to the extent indicated by the proposal will do serious harm to the businesses that rely on tourism and the tourism dollars which of course are generated by tourist travellers using the VIA Rail trains.
This hatchet job to VIA Rail will compromise the future of Canada's tourism industry and its ability to service the international tourism market.
Killing VIA Rail, Mr. Speaker, is indeed a false economy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the release of the GST technical paper has sparked considerable interest in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton. It has spawned an insatiable appetite for information. Over the past weeks I have attempted to meet this demand with a wide variety of materials. Public forums, talk shows, personal newspaper columns and briefing packages, as well as finance publications have all been made readily available to my constituents.
In the end they are appreciative of my efforts and the information that they are receiving; information that depicts the inequities of the current system, information that gives them a better understanding and appreciation of how the GST will work and benefit our country, information that allows them to know and understand that the present FST is hidden and the GST will be very, very evident.

I think that we all can learn an important lesson from my experience. We as members of Parliament have a duty to provide our constituents with as much factual information as possible on the GST. Only from this type of knowledge base can they formulate fair, accurate and informative opinions.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of all members and all Canadians the fact that September 1, 1989 marks the fiftieth anniversary of Nazi Germany's invasion of Poland. With this tragic invasion one-half century ago the world was plunged into war.
The memory of the horrifying consequences that followed serve to remind all of us of the importance of maintaining peace in the world. It reminds us also of the priority we must place in offering assistance in resolving conflict among other nations through the UN and whatever other means are available to us.
Canada and its allies came to the defence of the Polish people during the Second World War and we, along with other nations, paid a heavy price. Many of our youth never returned to enjoy the life of prosperity that we have experienced in Canada since then. We have not forgotten those fallen heroes who ensured our continuing freedom.
And we also recognize that the Polish people persevere in their struggle for freedom and democracy 50 years later. Their persistence through the years brought some progress, and we rejoiced with the Polish people when we saw the recent election of Solidarity members to the Government of Poland.
On this the fiftieth anniversary of their loss of freedom we salute the courageous people of Poland who go on with their fight, and we wish them continued success.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 1, 1989 it was discovered that 27 bags of mail, some of it postmarked as early as December 1988, had remained undelivered in a privatized postal outlet in Woodbridge, Ontario. Upon learning of this, the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, or CUPW, reported the incident to the media and then of course
Canada Post quickly picked up the mail bags and commenced a damage control exercise.
Canada Post management then launched a grievance against the union accusing CUPW of "direct public criticism detrimental to the corporation's legitimate business interests".
This is simply nuts. Canada Post should have thanked the union for reporting the error and should have apologized to the people of Canada for the sloppy service. But, typically of Canada Post, it chose instead to shoot the messenger.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a single country made up of different cultures in different regions. Sometimes people forget this and try to drive wedges between us.
Yesterday Canadian Press reported that a member of this national House went to Quebec during the recent election campaign. While there he was quoted as saying disparaging, divisive and unsettling things about Quebec and Quebecers. At a time when all regions of the country are feeling political pressures to pull in their own narrow self-interest this was a distressing report.
If anywhere, national unity has to be felt on the floor of the House of Commons. If anyone speaks for Canada it has to be members of Parliament. So I salute the member, my colleague here, for accepting this reality and apologizing to this House.
You are either for Canada or you are against Canada, and that means all of it. Linguistic tolerance, as my colleague has just said, is the cornerstone this country is built on. None of us can afford to forget that, even for a moment.

Mr. Speaker, the decision last week by this government to move search and rescue from CFB Summerside to Nova Scotia certainly jeopardizes the work of the federal-provincial task force.
When this task force was set up by the federal government to examine the base closure, search and rescue was on the table for discussion. Now the government has chosen to ignore the process which it helped to set up.
I would urge the Department of National Defence to postpone any decision regarding CFB Summerside until
September 27, 1989

the task force has submitted its report. Otherwise it will continue to undermine and compromise the credibility and the usefulness of this task force.
The people of Prince Edward Island are fed up with this kind of conduct.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to comment on the government's plan to axe the passenger rail service in this country. British Columbians are accustomed to being ignored but we will not take it quietly.
VIA cuts to B.C. include reduction of the Transcontinental, elimination of the winter run on the Jasper-Prince Rupert line, and total disappearance of E & N passenger service on Vancouver Island. The E & N is near and dear to my heart. The island has always been my home. Some 9,000 people from only two federal ridings on Vancouver Island sent in petitions demanding that the E & N be saved; saved, expanded and run efficiently.
If VIA Rail had been running all its lines the way it has the E & N, no one can doubt that VIA management has played directly into the government hands. It has run its service so badly that anyone looking at the books would say "Shut it down".
I suggest this has been done deliberately in order to provide this government with the excuse it has been seeking. Some 9,000 from a small part of Vancouver Island would like to be heard. How many across Canada? British Columbians demand open debate and public hearings to voice their views. The government must listen.

Mr. Speaker, in 1981 when the then Liberal government cut back Atlantic service the Conservatives claimed to be outraged. In 1985 they reinstated the Atlantic route and issued a challenge to Atlantic Canadians: "Use it or lose it". Some statement.
Atlantic Canadians took these words to heart and in 1988 close to a million passengers rode the rails in the maritimes. A target was set for the Atlantic route-200,000 riders by 1990. That challenge was met in 1987 when 249,000 Atlantic Canadians rode on the Atlantic route. That challenge was met again in 1988 And again in the first four months of this year that challenge was met.
Atlantic Canadians have lived up to their part of the bargain but the government has not. The Conservative government has once again deceived Atlantic Canadians. It plans to eliminate all train service except what amounts to a thrice weekly tourist run in that region of the country where VIA is the most popular, and that is unacceptable. I challenge this government to remember its commitment to Atlantic Canadians. They have used it. They don't deserve to lose it.

Mr. Speaker, the Soviet central authorities have clearly demonstrated that they are unable or unwilling to lift a month long Azerbaijani blockade of Karabagh and Armenia. The delivery of desperately needed materials for the reconstruction of the earthquake stricken regions of Armenia has been blocked by Azerbaijani. In March of this year I saw the destruction and the suffering caused by the earthquake, and I believe that manipulating that tragedy for political ends is unacceptable.
I call on our government to bring the present critical situation to the attention of the UN General Assembly and other competent organs of the United Nations, to appeal to the Soviet authorities urgently to lift the blockade of Armenia and Karabagh, to ensure the security of the Armenian people in the region and, lastly, to organize a referendum in mountainous Karabagh in

September 27, 1989
Oral Questions
order to ascertain the majority will of the autonomous region.

Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary committee studying the unemployment insurance bill, Bill C-21, is now in its fourth week of intensive hearings. As of last night 143 out of the 183 groups appearing before the committee in all provinces have strenuously opposed this bill. That is overwhelming opposition.
These groups have pointed out that the cuts proposed in the bill will leave 775,000 unemployed Canadians with no or reduced unemployment insurance benefits. The only alternative for these Canadians will be provincial or municipal social welfare.
When will the Conservative government start listening to the grassroots of this country and withdraw this bill, send it back to the drawing board and present new legislation which will effectively help, not hurt, Canada's unemployed?

Mr. Speaker, this week the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Secretary of State for Canada, and the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Education announced that Canada will soon ratify the UNESCO convention on the recognition of studies and diplomas. They also announced that a commission for the international recognition of foreign studies and diplomas will be created to apply the convention in our country.
The main purpose of this convention is to share information about educational, scientific, and technological resources. The commission will collect information on the education systems of other countries and make it available in Canada. It will also promote our education system internationally.
We welcome the efforts of the commission in the work it will carry out in the interests of fellow Canadians of all origins who have completed their schooling elsewhere. Their qualifications are not always fully recognized. The commission's work will help reduce such inequities by
providing up to date and objective information to those who are involved in the recognition of foreign academic credentials.
Let us join in congratulating the ministers responsible for this excellent example of federal-provincial collaboration in an initiative that will benefit all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Transport arrogantly refused to meet a delegation of this country's mayors to discuss the future of VIA Rail. The Prime Minister also should know that there are reports right across Canada today that at the very time the minister refused to meet our mayors he was at a cabinet meeting recommending the elimination of VIA routes to Sydney, Yarmouth, Ed-mundston, Sherbrooke, Brantford, Sarnia, London, and Trois Rivieres.
There are also reports that the minister recommended the elimination of the Halifax-Montreal train service. There are documents to the effect that the minister recommended destroying our most famous train service, The Canadian, from Montreal to Vancouver, across the Canadian Shield, through the prairies and across the Rocky Mountains.
I want to say to the Prime Minister, because we get nothing from his minister, that the time for cat and mouse games played with this House of Commons is over. Will the Prime Minister finally tell Canadians, or order his minister to tell Canadians, what cuts are in store for them on the service of VIA Rail and do it before this Parliament finally runs that minister out of town on a rail?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, the Leader of the Opposition is wrong. I met the mayors of municipalities twice in June for a long time. I think they had a chance to express exactly what they wanted to express.
September 27, 1989

As I said yesterday, the Leader of the Opposition speaks out of both sides of his mouth. He said I refused to consult but he asked me to make a decision immediately. I believe we have to make up our minds. I will make a decision on official documents, not the one that the Leader of the Opposition is referring to. I issued no official document about the decision. When it is made I will be pleased to give official documents to the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, returning again to the documents that are abroad in the country today, it is bad enough that the Minister of Transport recommended eliminating VIA Rail service from Winnipeg to Brandon to Regina to Calgary, but he actually recommended that the only train service available from Toronto to Niagara Falls be Amtrak, the American passenger rail service.
How could the Prime Minister continue to justify having in his cabinet a Minister of Transport who recommends that Ontario and the Niagara Peninsula be served only by the American national train service?

Mr. Speaker, any representations the Minister of Transport has to make in the decision-making process are made in Cabinet. That is the procedure and it is the procedure I intend to follow, But I repeat, as I said in English, that I think it is essential, and the Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that in the decision-making process, decisions are not made on the basis of leaked documents but on the basis of official documents. And that is what I intend to do. When the decision is made, I will be happy to give him some documents, but these will be official documents.

I think on this issue Canadians have come to the conclusion that enough is enough. American Express is going to run our banks and Amtrak is now going to run our rail service. Canadians are beginning to wonder when the United States postal service is going to deliver our mail. That is what Canadians are waiting for.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the Minister mentioned consultation. Yesterday, the Prime Minister said here in the House how important the Finance Committee's hearings were for the future of his sale tax. However, his Minister of Transport, despite what he said today, tells us there will be no public hearings to determine the future of VIA Rail. I therefore have the following question for the Prime Minister: Does he intend to disown his Minister of Transport who, in the past few days, has shown utter contempt for the public consultation process? Will the Prime Minister guarantee that no cutbacks will be imposed on VIA Rail without regular, public consultation with Canadians across the country?

Mr. Speaker, I will repeat what I said earlier. The reference levels for VIA Rail were given to the Department of Transport last April. It is now the end of September, and during that time I met dozens of people. I met mayors, and last week I had a meeting with the provincial ministers. I consulted, and I even had meetings with Members of the Opposition. So in that context, I think that any information that was out there was received. I repeat, a decision will be made as soon as we feel it is necessary to do so and we will communicate that decision, and this will be done, I repeat, according to the normal procedure, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. The
7,000	people who work for VIA Rail, whose livelihoods depend upon VIA Rail, and the millions of Canadians who support a rail passenger service in this country have a right to be heard on the future of VIA Rail.
This question has never been referred to the Commons transport committee for public hearings and it has never been referred to the National Transportation Agency for public hearings.
My question for the Prime Minister is quite simple. Yesterday the Prime Minister himself, on the floor of this House, made a strong case that it was critical in the case of the goods and services tax that the Commons finance committee be heard and that the government give the committee a chance to work and consider its recommendations. If the Prime Minister's principle of yesterday meant anything, will he tell this House today

September 27, 1989
Oral Questions
that the future of VIA Rail will be referred for full public hearings to the Commons transport committee and to the appropriate regulatory agency, the National Transportation Agency? Will he do that today?

Mr. Speaker, I myself met with the committee on transport twice in May or June. The committee can have the discussions it wants. It is up to the committee to do what it wants, but at the same time I repeat what I said, that for six months now we have considered a lot of representations from VIA Rail.
Something is clear. The Minister of Finance, I think quite relevantly, has decided for the best of this country to determine new reference levels for VIA Rail, for a mode of transportation that only 3 per cent of Canadians use. I will make a decision within the fiscal responsibility. I think that is what Canadians want.

Mr. Speaker, "how ironic", in the words of Mayor Elsie Wayne on behalf of 24 mayors who received a collective slap in the face yesterday.
They were left waiting in the Railway Committee Room of the House of Commons for a Minister of Transport and/or a Prime Minister who never showed up. In her words, "how ironic to have a Prime Minister, who on the one hand professes to admire the glasnost of the Soviet Union, practising a dictatorial tactic in this country".
My question for the Prime Minister is quite simple. He has not answered it. Yesterday the Prime Minister said it was an important principle of parliamentary democracy that the Standing Committee on Finance of the House of Commons be heard on an important national matter like the goods and services tax before the government acted.
If he is consistent and sincere, will he give a commitment in this House today that the Commons transport committee and the National Transportation Agency will hold public hearings on the future of VIA Rail before this government brings down the axe?

Mr. Speaker, in regard to glasnost and perestroika I would just tell my hon. friend in regard to VIA Rail and VIA Rail hearings that unless I am badly mistaken he was a member of the government which in 1981 walked in and, without so much as a single hearing, wiped out 20 per cent of VIA Rail service across the country.
Not only did they do it, they did it on a Friday night in the middle of summer. They did not even have the courage to confront the House of Commons. I think this is an absolutely shameful thing to have done.
The Minister of Transport is a model of consultation in a democracy compared with the Liberals.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a question for the Prime Minister in the absence of a Minister of Transport who neither knows nor cares about transportation in this country.
The Prime Minister has just reminded this House of the Liberal tactic of passing an Order in Council in the middle of the summer on a Friday afternoon in order to cut 20 per cent. It was the Minister of Transport's intention, as he told the Transport Committee, to do the same thing in the middle of this summer. Only his dithering has prevented that from occurring. I want to ask the Prime Minister-
Oh, oh!

The Tory caucus may think this is funny, but to the seven million Canadians who use VIA Rail it is damned important.
I want the Prime Minister to indicate whether or not the priorities and planning committee of cabinet did consider this document that was referred to in the Winnipeg Free Press this morning, and if so, did P and P approve the recommendations to go to cabinet or did it reject them.

Mr. Speaker, I will first of all say to my friend that he knows very well that he asked me not to make a decision this summer. The decision has not been made. It is exactly as he wanted, and he is not happy again. I do not understand.
The process of decision by the cabinet is not made on leaked documents. That is very clear. I believe once again that what my friend wants to know is when the decision will be made. I will be pleased to tell him. But at the time I will give him official documents so the question could be more relevant to me in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, we have been asking for those documents for a long time. The people of Canada would like to see them before the decision is made and
September 27, 1989

before the Order in Council is passed, because at that point it becomes law.
If P and P has not made the decision, perhaps the Prime Minister could explain why over 130 VIA Rail employees were served notice of permanent lay-offs this morning, some of them with over 20 years of seniority and nothing to rely on. Could he explain how that decision is happening in the absence of any kind of cabinet decision?

Mr. Speaker, the decision about VIA Rail has been made within the current operations of the corporation. They are working at the present time. The corporation wants to operate within the reference levels we have given. They did before. Years before there were no decisions as we have to make. They will do it again. Regardless of the fact that we have to make decisions today, those people have been laid off in the regular process of the operations of a Crown corporation. That is all.

That is a regular process according to the Tory philosophy, I think.
Mr. Speaker, my final question is to the Prime Minister. Again I want to go back to him because we have a Minister of Finance who is dictating the monetary aspects of VIA Rail. We have a Minister of Transport who is taking the approach of elimination of service. I want him to accept his responsibility. I ask the Prime Minister if, finally, he will appoint a cabinet minister responsible for transportation who believes in rail passenger services, not just in air and road transportation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think I believe as much as the member believes in rail transportation. But, in my view, it is not necessary to put $700 million into a service which is not used by Canadians. Only the NDP do not worry about where we get the money. You can expend the money. I am trying to see where I would best spend the money for all transportation in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. This country has had experience with leaked documents. One of them became a Budget.
Oral Questions
This leaked document will mean the loss of 180 out of 210 jobs in the city of Moncton. That makes a total of
2,000	people who have lost their jobs in Moncton over the last two years.
This government is interested in freight and not people. They have hearings for CN abandonment of lines, but they do not have them for VIA.
Given the Minister of Transport's refusal to meet the mayor of Moncton yesterday, will the Prime Minister give his commitment for full public transportation committee hearings in Moncton and across this country?

Mr. Speaker, I have already answered that question. I said that I met with the mayors of Saint John and Mississauga. If you are from Ontario, you will know very well that when the mayor of Mississauga has something to say she does not need to say it twice. We understand it very well the first time.
I would like to say as well that I believe consultations have been made. We have to make a decision. The people of New Brunswick, like everyone else in the country, have had the chance to make their views known, and I have taken them into account. Now it is time for a decision.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is to the Prime Minister. Given that two million passengers use VIA in the Windsor-Quebec corridor representing 17 per cent of the travelling public, and given that Samia-London represents the gateway to Chicago and the mid-west with its great tourist potential, how can this government with its perverted logic even consider cutting VIA service to the corridor?
Mr. Speaker, very shortly we will know exactly the future of VIA Rail-when the decision will be made. It is just speculation and premature to say what he said.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. We have read that the west is losing The Canadian, our nation's original transcontinental train. We have also read that the Minister of Transport is recommending a so-called luxury service connecting Toronto to Calgary.

September 27, 1989
Oral Questions
Will the Prime Minister tell us today which of his good friends in the private sector will be picking up passengers in Brandon, Kenora, Moose Jaw, Swift Current, Maple Creek, Medicine Hat and many other communities across the west that he is forcing VIA Rail to abandon?

Mr. Speaker, once again, the decisions concerning VIA Rail are made following a normal procedure and certainly not based on documents that no one has seen, leaked documents, documents which, again, have not been submitted to me. In this context, any information of that kind is not serious and is not to be considered.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of State for Transport. Does the Minister of State, who is southern Ontario's voice in cabinet, agree with and support the cuts to VIA Rail in an area where the highways and skyways are already congested and clogged? How can she stay in cabinet under these circumstances?
Mr. Speaker, as the voice in cabinet for southern Ontario, and as the Minister of Transport has said, we do not comment on leaked documents. When the decisions are made, then I will make my comments.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Is he awake over there?
This Conservative government said to the people of the Atlantic region regarding rail passenger service, "Use it or lose it". In fact, VIA passenger ridership this year to date is up 30 per cent. The people of the Atlantic have kept their end of the bargain.
My question to the minister is this. Will the minister now keep his end of the bargain with the people of the Atlantic and assure them that there will be no slashing or cutting or gypping of Atlantic Canadians of their rail passenger service?

Mr. Speaker, when I was the Minister of Employment this member was my critic. I think he was a little more serious, because I have already answered that question.
I said, of course, if we consider the philosophy of his party, we will expend all the money we can without giving thought to where we will get the money. We believe Canadians want a system of transportation which is national, which can give the services to Canadians with the affordability we have and in a way that will sustain all transportation systems in the country. That is what we are trying to provide to all Canadians, Mr. Speaker.

My supplementary is to the same minister. I recall that when I was the critic for employment and immigration this minister was a lot more serious and thoughtful about unemployment matters.
In view of the fact that Atlantic Canadians are finding themselves increasingly isolated from this government, first with budget cuts, then with GST, with back-benchers who make all sorts of insulting remarks about Atlantic Canadians, Summerside and a whole host of other matters, I want to give the minister this opportunity, to get on the better side of Atlantic Canadians-one more opportunity, one more try. Can the minister stand in his place and assure Atlantic Canadians that there will be no cut-backs in VIA Rail service in the future?

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member for Nickel Belt that I will try to manage the Department of Transport in a way that respects the reference levels which have been given to me by the Minister of Finance in light of the fiscal reality of Canada. I believe, as a responsible minister, I have to take into account the reality of the economy of Canada. I have to work out any option which will permit Atlantic Canada, central Canada or western Canada to respect that purpose. It is what I will do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Over the last number of months over 200,000 Atlantic Canadians have signed petitions opposing any cut-back in VIA Rail service. All four Atlantic premiers have said that they are opposed to such cuts.
Yesterday, in a monumental display of ignorance and contempt, the Minister of Transport refused to meet with Mayor Elsie Wayne and 24 other municipal leaders from across Canada to discuss this very serious issue. Since the Minister of Transport says that he has consulted enough, then either the Minister of Transport is
September 27, 1989

deaf or he is so arrogant that he has refused to listen. Mr. Prime Minister, which is it?

Mr. Speaker, I think once again that it is not arrogant to say that I met Mayor Wayne from New Brunswick. I met also Mayor McCal-lion from Mississauga. I met a lot of people.
But once again I repeat what I said. I think it is time to make a decision. That is what we will do, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, given that regional rail service out of Halifax is gone, given that students and seniors and the sick will have no recourse, and given most particularly that this government has wreaked more havoc on Halifax and Nova Scotia than the explosion of 1917, I ask the Prime Minister why has he singled out Halifax and Nova Scotia to be blown off the rails?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, once again I ask the hon. member to wait for the decision, wait for the decision and she will have the time to make her comments after. But for now, wait, Mr. Speaker. Wait for the decision, please.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of Mr. Michael Harris, Member of the Ontario Legislature and Progressive Conservative House Leader.

Mr. Speaker, several weeks ago, we heard Finance Department officials tell us that the cost of food in Canada could go down by about 2 per cent. We no longer hear such affirmations. Instead, Mr. Speaker, we hear food companies talk about food costs increasing by 10 to 13 per cent, if the GST base is broadened.
My question for the Minister of Finance is this: Given Canadians' concerns and their fierce opposition to any tax on food, can the Minister of Finance tell us today, categorically and clearly, that there will be no food tax in Canada?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I believe that I have commented on that particular question on a number of occasions in the House. I do not propose to do so again.
I would say that the comments the hon. member is referring to about the possible increase in the cost of food that we referred to yesterday in the committee hearings are based clearly on a guesstimate of what costs might be incurred. I think he will understand that there are offsets to those costs because of the fact that food will not be taxable under the proposal, and that in the proposal there will be credits that food companies will receive. So they will see some of their costs reduced as well.

Mr. Speaker, a lot things are being said about the cost of food in Canada, but particularly my question to the Minister is this. Senior citizens in this country feel that they have been under attack for the last four or five years. There have been deindexation of pensions, increasing costs across the board and a claw-back scheme.
Now it seems to me only reasonable that the minister could soothe those fears by standing in his place and stating very clearly to Canadians that under no circumstances will his government tax food. That is a very simple plea on the part of Canadians who feel they have been under serious attack by this government over the last four or five years. Can he say clearly in the House, no, there will be no tax on food for Canadians, seniors or otherwise?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I believe that we have responded to the concern that senior citizens have expressed with the proposal that is before the House today. I want to remind the hon. member of the ways in which we have attempted to design the package with the concerns and the interests of senior citizens very much in mind. There is the exemption of basic groceries. There are the other exemptions on medical devices, prescription drugs, health care services, non-profit homemaker services and meals-on-wheels. All of these things were designed and put specifically in the goods and services tax package to directly address the concerns of senior citizens.

Hear, hear!
Oral Questions
September 27, 1989

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. It has been five months since the announced closing of CFB Portage. With that closure the minister announced that the department was going to secure private pilot training capability. I would like to know if the minister has acted on that promise, and if he is considering Portage La Prairie to train the defence pilots.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question and also for his assistance in seeking meaningful economic activity in his community.
With respect to the primary training that is presently done at Portage, we sent out a solicitation of interest to some 260 companies around the world, including several in Canada. We received replies and expressions of interest from some 57. Those are being reviewed now. I can inform the hon. member that several of those expressions of interest included use of existing facilities presently in Canada. After the evaluation has been concluded, I am sure that I will be able to announce to the House and to those interested, the decisions that will be made.

Mr. Speaker, I have a rather sensitive question for the Prime Minister of Canada. I want to know whether or not the chairman of the finance committee was stating government policy when he said yesterday, after seniors appeared before the committee, and I quote, "They, seniors, live at a slower pace and they do not spend money in the same sense that you and I do. Older people don't wear out their clothes, don't wear out their furniture, don't run around, and all that costs money".
I want to know whether or not the chairman of the finance committee was enunciating government policy concerning senior citizens who have built this country and who have paid their taxes. Does he owe them an apology? I want him to get up in this House now and say that he apologizes for this kind of a statement.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to speak on behalf of the chairman of the finance committee.
Oh, oh!

The chairman of the finance Committee may or may not have expressed those views. I do not know whether or not he is quoted out of context.
Clearly, as I indicated to a previous question, the concerns of senior citizens have very much been taken into account as we have designed a package for the goods and services tax. I will not repeat the various ways we have done so. But, clearly, if one takes an objective view of the various ways we have responded to those concerns, I think that senior citizens would say this package is a very solid and very sensitive one for the senior citizens of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a laughing matter. What I want to know from the chairman of the finance committee is whether or not he was speaking on behalf of the Minister of Finance, whether or not he was speaking on behalf of the Government of Canada when he said that older people don't wear out their clothes, don't wear out their furniture, don't run around, and all that costs money. Will he now apologize to the senior citizens of this country?

Mr. Speaker. I last had the opportunity to speak on this particular bill on June 22 before the House adjourned for the summer break. I understand that I have some 10 or 12 minutes to conclude my remarks. In order to put my concluding remarks into perspective, permit me to repeat some of the submissions I made on June 22, 1989.
We are here today as we were then to discuss in principle Bill C-18. The purpose of second reading debate is to determine whether, in a general way, in principle, this House ought to endorse and support a particular piece of legislation. This piece of legislation, Bill. C-18, is an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and to amend certain acts in relation thereto.
Let me say in no uncertain terms that I believe very fundamentally that this bill ought not to be approved in principle. I would like to explain the reasons why. I do
not believe that the Government of Canada should be establishing a Department of Multiculturalism.
Up until now, it has been the policy of the Government of Canada, from 1971, that Canada would be a bilingual and multicultural country. The policy of multiculturalism was introduced by a previous Liberal administration in 1972. While at the time and in the subsequent years that particular policy may have been of benefit to immigrant Canadians and to Canada generally, I believe very strongly that the policy is no longer appropriate or valid today. In effect, the present policy of multiculturalism is divisive. It divides Canadians. It is unfair in that it treats Canadians in a different fashion. It is regressive and at times discriminatory. Let me explain why I feel that way. If one were to ask Canadians generally what they thought multiculturalism was and if one were to ask members of Parliament to explain what multiculturalism means, they would say, I suspect, that it means everything other than French or English. If you are a French Canadian and you are not part of the multicultural community, or if you are an English Canadian or an anglophone, you are not part of the multicultural community. However, if you have origins that are Italian, Greek, German, East Indian or South American, then somehow you are part of that multicultural community. You are "an ethnic".
In the true sense of the word, multicultural means everybody. My French Canadian colleagues here in the House of Commons are just as much a part of the multicultural community as I am as a Canadian of Italian origin. That is not the mindset here in Ottawa today and indeed throughout the country. When one speaks of multiculturalism in this House of Commons, one is speaking of Canadians who have origins other than French or English. In many ways, that is discriminatory because there is almost a suggestion that because one is part of the multicultural community, somehow one is inferior, is of a different class, is of inferior quality to Canadians who have origins that are French or English.
I was bom in Canada. My parents are immigrants to this country. They came to Canada in 1950 from Italy. I was bom in Revelstoke, British Columbia. I do not consider myself a francophone. I do not consider French to be my mother tongue. I have no origins that relate to things French. I do not consider myself an anglophone
September 27, 1989

even though I speak English fluently and English was the language of my education. So I ask myself, what am I?
If I am not a francophone and not an anglophone and the Government of Canada seems to suggest in its policies and legislation that it is either one or the other, then I am in a category which is multicultural. I am in the basket over here that consists of everyone with roots other than French or English.
We are bilingual because of history and because the English and the French were the first settlers. Far be it from me to give a history lesson today, but that is why we are bilingual and have a policy of bilingualism in Canada. The arguments for bilingualism are strong.
One also has to accept what Canada is today and what Canada is becoming. What will the Canada of the future be? Statistics Canada recently reported that 34 per cent of Canadians have origins that are British, and that number is diminishing. Twenty-four per cent of Canadians have origins that are French, so 58 per cent of Canadians have origins that are French or English. Of the remainder, 25 per cent have origins other than French or English and 5 per cent have origins that are a mixture of French, British and some other origin. The reality today is that the country is more diverse than it ever was.
Of the immigrant population in Canada, people who migrated to Canada, one-half arrived in Canada before 1967 and one-third arrived between 1967 and 1977. Less than 20 per cent arrived in Canada since 1977.
The reality is that those of us who have origins other than French or English have just as much right, just as much entitlement to equal protection and equal benefit of the law as defined by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Mr. Speaker, you have indicated that my time is nearly up. I will appreciate the opportunity to answer any questions that my colleagues might have.
It is a step backward to start entrenching multicultur-alism. We ought to be moving to the next phase, to recognize what Canada is today and what Canada will be in the future for our children and grandchildren. We as Canadians have to start talking about a new national spirit, a spirit that says that we are all Canadians.

I frankly am tired of being a hyphenated Canadian. I am not a hyphenated Canadian. I am fiercely proud of my heritage. I will defend my heritage and promote my heritage, but I am a Canadian. I am not an Italian-Cana-dian or a Canadian-Italian. I happen to be a Canadian of Italian origin. I am very proud of my heritage and I am proud of the fact that I am Canadian. I suspect that the one-third of Canadians who have origins other than French or English feel as I do.
I think it is time that we stopped segregating and ghettoizing Canadians of origins other than French or English and that we all start talking about and promoting what we all have in common and that is the fact that we are Canadian. Whether we come from Quebec, whether we have origins that are British, Japanese, German, Italian, Greek, or whatever, we are all Canadians. To support this bill in principle is to take a tremendous step backward. I urge colleagues not to support this bill in principle and to refer it back to the government to bring in a piece of legislation that will recognize the equality of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for York South-Weston on his deep concern for the multicultural communities of Canada and for the country that Canada has become. I would like him to elaborate for this House on one of the matters that he has raised most forcefully with us, his colleagues on this side of the House. It is the question of the redress to the Japanese-Canadians and the way it was handled by the government.
He has brought forth to us the point that this matter was considered a multicultural issue. It was handled by the minister responsible for multiculturalism as opposed to other ministers who are more properly charged with questions of fundamental justice, fundamental human rights and the way we treat people, not because of their ethnic origin or their background or their language but simply because they are Canadians, simply because they are human beings. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for York South-Weston to elaborate on this point and to continue his remarks.

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in my remarks, the policy of multiculturalism as embraced by this government and as introduced by the previous Liberal administration is discriminatory. I use as an example the way the Japanese Canadian redress ques-

September 27, 1989
Government Orders
tion was handled by the House of Commons and by the government in particular over the last number of years.
Because Canadians of Japanese origin are not anglophones or francophones and because they are a visible minority, the mindset in this Parliament and the mindset on the government side was that anything having to with Canadians of Japanese origin must be an issue involving multiculturalism.
If that is not the ultimate insult and the classic example of how discriminatory the policy of multiculturalism is, I do not know what is.
That issue ought to have been dealt with by the Minister of Justice. As my colleague quite eloquently pointed out, it was an issue of natural justice and a matter that ought to have been dealt with by the government as a policy not having to do with ethnic origin but having everything to do with justice.
The mindset on that side of the House was because they have origins that are Japanese, hand the issue over to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism. I ask rhetorically what the reaction would have been in Canada if the Government of Canada had handed over the issue of Nazi war criminals to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism. I do not believe that would have been acceptable.
I do not make these submissions in order to place blame but simply to reflect the negative mindset that exists in Ottawa with respect to the policy of multiculturalism.
I will use one more example, and again I do not mean to be critical. When Air India flight 182 was bombed off the coast of Ireland some five years ago, the initial reaction of the Government of Canada was to phone Rajiv Gandhi, the Prime Minister of India, to offer condolences to the families of the deceased.
It is necessary to ask why the Government of Canada called Rajiv Gandhi and the Government of India. The reason was that it was an Air India flight and because those on board wore turbans; some were Sikhs, others were darker in complexion because they were Hindus. There was a mindset that because these people were visible minorities, somehow they were not Canadian. The fact is that the overwhelming majority, in fact almost
all of those people who perished, were Canadian, but the government's multicultural mindset led it to call Rajiv Gandhi, the Prime Minister of India.
In answer to my colleague, I am saying that this policy of multiculturalism, not in a deliberate way but in an insidious way, is extremely discriminatory and insulting to those of us who have origins other than French or English. For that reason, I do not believe we ought to be supporting the perpetuation of a policy that treats our fellow Canadians as being inferior.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying that I have reviewed the speeches made when Bill C-18 was debated first. I noted that the first three speakers for the Liberal party spoke in favour of the principle of this bill and supported this bill. The NDP critic supported this bill. I am absolutely astounded that this member would be speaking against a multicultural bill to establish a new department which is going to oversee the Multiculturalism Act.
I would like to point out to the House that the Multiculturalism Act is multiculturalism for all Canadians, and that is part of the preamble of that act. I would like to say that the hon. member for York South-Weston voted for that act. The Multiculturalism Act states that it is for all Canadians and he voted for it. Now he is standing up here saying that the Multiculturalism Act divides Canadians.
I know that the Liberal party is having a great deal of difficulty with unity, but it is absolutely unbelievable that a group of people who have spent some time governing this country is now in total shambles in terms of its multiculturalism policy.
I would like to know from this member of Parliament how he can possibly be against this bill. I know that there is going to be a tremendous number of people in our city of metro Toronto who are going to be astounded at these comments.
I just read in one of the newspapers that the member said that multiculturalism is a fraud perpetrated on groups of ethnics other than French or English in order to appease them. Is that the policy of the Liberal party? He said that our current multicultural policy actually breeds racism in Canada because we are telling them they are different.
September 27, 1989

The Multiculturalism Act is about bringing people together, uniting people and I am positively astounded. I am sure there is embarrassment in the Liberal Party of Canada today because of this member's comments.

Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that the member is so easily astounded. It is obvious that the member was not listening to my submissions and that she does not have a full and complete understanding of the issue.
Yes, indeed, there may be members on my side of the House who support in principle this particular piece of legislation. I am telling you in no uncertain terms how I feel about this particular bill.
I was elected by the people of York South-Weston to come to this House of Parliament to express my point of view and I have done that. I have told you how I feel regardless of how the government feels, how the New Democratic Party feels or how other people feel about this particular legislation.
Rather than talking about the merits of my submissions, the member from Toronto is more interested in making a personal attack. I am prepared to debate with the member and she can establish the venue. If she wants to organize a meeting in metropolitan Toronto, I am prepared to debate her or anybody else who supports the bill on the merits of this particular piece of legislation.
The member for Scarborough Centre is sadly mistaken in her submissions. I have always expressed this particular point of view that I have expressed today. She said a few moments ago that multiculturalism means everybody, that it tends to unite. Why then would you have one ministry of multiculturalism and another of culture and communications? speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
I was pleased today when the House leader brought forth the motion to have the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship established, and we look forward to the participation of the members of the House of Commons on that committee. In the debate last June the Secretary of State outlined the important principle behind this legislation. Both opposition critics have also expressed their support for the bill and I believe it is important now, Mr. Speaker, to move this legislation from this chamber into committee where we can study it and have further discussion and examination.
As the minister noted when he introduced this bill, C-18 speaks to the future of Canada, a future where all Canadians are free to participate and to succeed in our society, a future that recognizes the words of Canada's first Canadian-born Governor General, Vincent Massey, when he said: "This country is more than a chain of wheat fields and mineral mines and pulpwood forests, it is more than even the union of ten provinces, it is the expression of a certain idea."
The bill before us today is the reaffirmation of that idea. C-18 establishes a new department of multiculturalism and citizenship that will administer the Multiculturalism Act, the Citizenship Act, and will also incorporate into one department a number of programs that are vital to the future of Canada, programs such as the national literacy strategy, a partnership program that is designed to address the tragedy of illiteracy in our society. Our government has set forth $110 million and through the literacy secretariat thousands of Canadian businesses, community organizations, and non-profit groups are becoming involved in fighting the problem of illiteracy.
I was honoured recently to attend a performance entitled Reading the Signs which is a play produced by a group of young actors that is touring schools and commu-

September 27, 1989
Government Orders
nity centres to promote literacy. This play, Reading the Signs, is being sponsored by both the federal government and a variety of business organizations.
Another aspect of this department will be voluntary action programs which support the outstanding work of hundreds of thousands of volunteers in Canada. Another will be human rights, and especially race relations which is becoming such an important issue in cities like metropolitan Toronto. The new department will also focus on citizenship registration and citizenship promotion. Recently there was a citizenship court ceremony which was attended by a group of Girl Guides who took out their citizenship registration as their way of promoting the vital aspects of citizenship.
Citizenship promotion is a central feature of C-18. Being Canadian is both an honour and a responsibility and the oath which every new citizen takes reads as follows:
I swear that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada, her heirs and successors according to law and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
As citizens we have the right and the duty to participate fully in every aspect of our society. We have the right to vote, to stand for public office, to travel abroad as Canadians and to enjoy the full economic benefits of our country. This year some 94,000 people will take the oath of Canadian citizenship with tremendous pride and declare themselves Canadians.
Recently I had the opportunity of opening the new citizenship court in Scarborough and it was such as privilege for me to speak at that ceremony. What a joy it is to participate in ceremonies where hundreds of people become Canadian citizens as a matter of choice. Later this week, Mr. Speaker, a very special citizenship ceremony will be held in Toronto for over 600 new Canadians of Chinese heritage who will take their Canadian citizenship.
The Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship created by this bill will help these new citizens and thousands like them as they move through the citizenship process. Clauses 4 and 5 of the bill outline the role of the minister in the department. The minister shall:
- promole among all members of Canadian society an understanding of the values inherent in Canadian citizenship and encourage participation in the social, cultural, political and economic life of Canada; and
(d)-promote among all members of Canadian society a greater awareness and understanding of human rights, fundamental freedoms and related values.
Those duties reflect on how we see ourselves as Canadians and this bill speaks to how we see our future as a dynamic and forward-looking society. This is not a bill merely to support organizations or to authorize existing programs of a government department. This is a bill that speaks for the value of our country.
Just over a year ago this chamber gave consent to the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. That act established in Canadian law the principle that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society. The Multiculturalism Act also declared that the policy of the Government of Canada is to recognize and promote the understanding that multiculturalism reflects the cultural and racial diversity of Canadian society and acknowledges the freedom of all members of Canadian society to preserve, enhance and share their cultural heritage.
Bill C-18 builds on the Multiculturalism Act by establishing a department to co-ordinate Canada's multiculturalism and citizenship programs. That co-ordination, however, is not exclusive to this department. The central principle of the Multiculturalism Act is that all government departments must be involved in the promotion of the pluralistic, free and open society.
The new department created by Bill C-18 is only part of the process. This is not a department of ethnicity, nor should it be. This is the department of being Canadian. This is a department that speaks to Canada's future and to the way that we see ourselves. This is a department that recognizes the richness and the benefits of Canadian life.
As a Conservative I believe very strongly in the importance of individual freedom; freedom for every woman and man in our society, regardless of race, religion, ethnic background or age, to succeed and prosper. Individual liberties and freedoms are the very essence of Conservative philosophy. Perhaps that philosophy is best expressed in the words of Prime Minister
September 27, 1989

John Diefenbaker when he said in the establishment of Canada's first Bill of Rights:
I am a Canadian, a free Canadian, free to speak without fear, free to worship God in my own way, free to stand for what I think is right, free to oppose what I believe wrong, free to choose those who shall govern my country. This heritage of freedom I pledge to uphold for myself and all mankind.
Bill C-18 supports and advances these principles. This bill creates a department that speaks to the very essence of what we are as a people and what we want to become as a people, looking forward to the promise of our shared future.
On July 1, Canadians celebrated the one hundred and twenty-second birthday of Confederation. In 1867 confederation brought together four disparate provinces to form Canada. Today we are forming a new confederation, a confederation of people who share a different culture and one future as a nation. The establishment of this new confederation of cultures was perhaps best expressed by a resident of Scarborough, an 11 year old boy, a recent immigrant to Canada. His name is Samuel Yip. He designed this year's Canada Day poster which read "Together we build Canada. Tous ensemble Canada.

I would just like to put some very simple and straightforward questions to the Hon. Member from Scarborough Centre. First, I would like her to define in clear terms what multiculturalism means. I would like her to explain why citizenship is such an integral part of this particular bill. She referred to it as essential. What is the relationship between multiculturalism and citizenship. Could she clearly define that relationship?
I would also like her to explain why when becoming a Canadian citizen it is important to swear allegiance to the Queen. She read the oath that must be sworn in order to become a Canadian citizen. I would like her to explain why someone coming from a non-Commonwealth country or someone who perhaps does not believe in the monarchy must swear allegiance to a non-Canadian of British origin before they become a Canadian.
Can I ask her finally to advise the House whether she considers herself an anglophone or a francophone or something else?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for that question. It gives me an opportunity to expand a little further on this issue-I suppose the issue of multiculturalism and citizenship. Why we need this department was probably best set out on September 15, 1988 when the Prime Minister stated that we would be establishing a new department of multiculturalism and citizenship. At that time he said "The decision to create a department of multiculturalism and citizenship recognizes that multiculturalism is a central feature of Canadian citizenship. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms entitles citizens from every ethnic and cultural background to exercise their freedom of choice, to retain their customs and honour their traditions while at the same time entering the mainstream of Canadian identity".
I think that sets out very well what we as a government are setting forth in terms of linking multiculturalism with citizenship.
In relation to the oath of office, each time I attend a citizenship court-and I have recently been attending quite a few across the country serving as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State-and each time that oath of citizenship is taken a special pride wells up in each of us about how fortunate we are to live in this great freedom-loving country. Our traditions and our history are based on that oath. If this member is indicating to the Canadian public that the Liberal party would not be wanting to swear allegiance to the Queen of Canada, I would like him to get in his place and say that because I think there would be a great many people across this country who would be most disturbed at that comment of the member.
I am sorry time is up and I cannot answer the rest of the questions but I would be pleased to discuss the matter further with the member.
