Mr. Speaker, I also feel proud and privileged to rise and speak today about this Bill C-18, an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
I would like to say at the outset in response to the remarks by the hon. member for York South-Weston that I too would, if I were of his mindset, be concerned. I think that it is a case of mindset, our attitude to citizenship, our attitude to cultures, our attitude to being a Canadian. We can take a mindset; in which we are concerned with discrimination, racism and bigotry but I do not think the hon. member's intentions are in that direction. I take the hon. member's intentions as being honourable and I regret that he is looking at this bill in what I would perceive to be a negative context. Of course because he is an elected public official, he is liable to lead in this negative context and that would be unfortunate because this is a bill to which you can attach a negative context if you wish, or it is one to which you can attach a very positive context.
I would prefer, frankly, to see this department called the department of Canadianism and citizenship. But I suppose there is a first step in this process. This country of ours, I am surprised to learn, is the first country in the world with a national multiculturalism piece of legislation. And so we are pioneering a process in Canada. We are pioneering a process, to some degree with our official languages policy which has been in place now both in New Brunswick and in Canada for 20 years or more. With the establishment of our Multiculturalism Act a year ago we have pioneered a piece of legislation on a world scale.
With respect to the linkage to our two official languages, to our English and our French, Bill C-93 last year, the act pertaining to Canadian multiculturalism states specifically in the recital that whereas the Constitution of Canada and the Official Languages Act provide that English and French are the official languages of Canada and neither abrogates nor derogates from any rights or privileges acquired or enjoyed with respect to any other language. It goes on to say in the purposes of the multicultural policy which that act describes: "(i) to preserve and enhance the use of languages other than English and French while strengthening the status and
use of the official languages of Canada". It further states: "(j) to advance multiculturalism throughout Canada in harmony with the national commitment to the official languages of Canada".
And so I have to reject vigorously the assertion by the hon. member from York South-Weston that this multiculturalism act is an isolation kind of an act that excludes anglophones and francophones or isolates those who are new Canadians and the like, as he has described them.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think that this bill is timely. There is great evidence of racism and bigotry in our nation and it is time that we as a Parliament addressed ourselves firmly and constructively to new visions in those directions.
In my home province of New Brunswick, Mr. Speaker, there are challenges today to the official languages policy of our province. There is an established party that has a specific, clear policy of unilingualism. And that same party has a policy of what it describes as selective immigration. It is not clear whether that selectivity excludes blacks, English, French, Chinese, or just exactly how selective it should be. They are the kinds of words that I find extremely troublesome.
As I say, while I sincerely do accept the honourable intentions from the member for York South-Weston, I would encourage him to apply his most positive perspective to this bill and to try to lead his constituents and to help us lead this country in a recognition of the purposes of this bill for the national unity which it intends to pursue.
It was about 20 years ago when New Brunswick officially adopted its policies of bilingualism making us then and now Canada's only such province. We have been distinctive and enriched by those policies over the years. It was not long after that, in 1973, that the New Brunswick Multicultural Association was bom in my city of Fredericton. It has flourished and it has also helped to make our society distinctive and enriched in New Brunswick.
Today, as I have said, there are challenges and we must defend against those challenges and we must inspire and lead our citizens to tolerance and recognition of the richness which the diversity of Canada brings to all Canadians. The bill before us today will bring to fruition
September 27, 1989

the promise made by the Prime Minister last September, as my colleague has said.
I have read this bill and considered it very closely. It is a bill about the future of Canada. It is a bill about where we as a society want to go and what we must do to achieve our objectives. This new department of multicul-turalism and citizenship will be a department about bringing Canadians together, about strengthening the values which we hold in common.

Mr. Speaker, two important factors that make us a distinct nation are our recognition of multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of our society and our recognition of two official languages.

Another factor is our generous and humane immigration policy, our willingness to share our homeland in intelligent and compassionate ways with the rest of the world.
In 1987 the projected level of 125,000 immigrants was exceeded and reached 152,098. Immigration levels under the Progressive Conservative Government policy in 1989 will be almost twice as high as those under the Liberals in 1984.
This department of multiculturalism and citizenship is intended to address those new Canadians. It is intended to give them a special attention, a special opportunity, a special interest by the Government of Canada and to bring to the attention of all Canadians the distinctive and enriching values which these new Canadians bring to our country, to ingrain them with the spirit of Canadianism while permitting and encouraging them to retain their original identities and the richness of their individual cultures and languages.
My point is that the government has demonstrated the will, the commitment and the determination to face contemporary social issues affecting all Canadians. This government has demonstrated the will to meet the challenges that are afforded by a multicultural society and to meet the challenges that are afforded by a bilingual Canada.
In closing I would like to say that preserving freedom is not an easy process. It is a process of give and take and it is a process of spirit and vision and leadership. The rights
Government Orders
of all Canadians to cultural identity and official language services are basic freedoms of Canadianism. They have been hard-fought and hard-won. We have an enormous responsibility to defend, to sustain, to lead and to enhance those freedoms which make our country so respected and so admired throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, the essence of citizenship and multiculturalism is truly equality and dignity among all Canadians. In the non-ideal world of today we need a department that will make this world a bit more perfect. The hon. member for York South-Weston thinks of the ideal world today and of course we have to respect his views.
At this juncture however I would like to call the attention of the government because the member for Scarborough Centre did say that our hon. member is an embarrassment. Well, the Minister for Multiculturalism last August in the Conservative Party convention did in essence say that his party, the Conservative Party, treats ethnic minorities with distrust and disdain. I saw the Minister for Multiculturalism was earlier in the House and I am a little unhappy that he had to leave. Of course I understand he may have to attend to another schedule. I would like him to explain how he came to his conclusion. It is proving to me that we are not living in an ideal world when the Conservative Party treats ethnic minorities with distrust and disdain. He said further that unless the Conservative Party cultivates the ethnic votes it could lose all the major metropolitan ridings in Canada in the next election. Is the Conservative party truly for multiculturalism or is it truly only for election votes? Is it an election ploy? He who is without sin, let him cast the first stone, it has been said.
Also, the member for Scarborough Centre said today, "We are forming a new confederation". Well, the ideal is excellent but if it is only today that we are beginning to form this new confederation we have missed the boat, we have missed history. The Liberal Party of Canada must be given credit for taking the initiative to institute the multiculturalism policy. Of course we have to continue to improve. That is the challenge to humanity all the time.
I agree with the member for Fredericton-York Sun-bury that the timeliness of this topic is here for reasons of racism, of unfair hiring practices, and of selected immigration. I am glad that the member for Frederic-

Government Orders
ton-York Sunbuiy did make those observations and I congratulate him for that.
So I support this bill. The Liberal Party of Canada supports this bill. Multiculturalism is here to stay in a non-ideal world and I only hope that the government, by enacting this bill, will truly give teeth to its proclamations, that henceforth there will be racial equality in this country, that there will be respect and dignity, that there will be jobs for all, and that the bill will not only be used as an election ploy.
As a new Canadian citizen, as a new member of Parliament, now I can feel very proud with all humility to participate in the debate of this honoured House. To contribute to this debate is my honour and I hope that the government will continue this policy of equality for all.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a lot of feeling that I get up to support the government on this bill. This bill is to establish a department of multiculturalism and citizenship. I think we should look at some of the specific duties that are outlined in it. I would like to take the liberty of reading some of them.
The bill's specific duties are to initiate, recommend, co-ordinate, implement and promote national policies and programs with respect to multiculturalism and citizenship; to provide services for the acquisition and proof of citizenship; to promote among all members of Canadian society an understanding of the values inherent in Canadian citizenship and encourage participation in the social, cultural, political and economic life of Canada; as well as to promote among all members of Canadian society a greater awareness and understanding of human rights, fundamental freedoms and related values.
Canada has a proud history in relation to multiculturalism and religious, political and racial freedom. It also has some very bleak history. I think there are many things that are significant within my own personal life that meet the implementation of this type of bill.
First of all, my father was an immigrant. He left Russia because of political and religious persecution. He came to Canada because he felt as a Canadian citizen he could follow his religious beliefs, that he would have the rights of a citizen to pursue his own way of life to gain
economic security and to raise a family. These promises were fulfilled. He was proud to be a Canadian citizen. He always treasured the fact that he was able to go to a citizenship court and take out his citizenship.
However, my wife is Canadian bom but of Japanese ancestry. She experienced as a young child that her Canadian citizenship was not worth anything. She was uprooted from her home, taken with her family and interned in the horse bams at the exhibition grounds in Vancouver-so much for her Canadian citizenship. Yet her father, in spite of those things, was always proud that he became Canadian. He valued the things that Canada stood for and valued the ideals that we have.
I live in the riding of Surrey North which is very much a multicultural riding. It is a riding which has a large number of immigrants. It has Portuguese, Scandinavians, Germans, people from the Latin American countries and people from India. I am now holding teas to welcome new immigrants. It is really a multicultural mosaic afternoon.
Many of my constituents, particularly those from the Punjab, do not have happy memories about the way they have been treated in Canada. Many of their relatives remember that in 1914 the Komagata Maru, containing 376 passengers, 340 of whom were Sikh, arrived in Vancouver. As they were all British subjects, they were entitled under Canadian law to enter Canada. However, when the ship arrived in Vancouver harbour, Canadian immigration officials denied them landing rights, severed communications to shore and denied permission to replenish their food and water, finally forcing the ship to leave and return to Indian waters. Needless to say, this incident deeply humiliated the Sikh community. It continues to be a source of national shame for Canada.
Surrey North is fortunate to have a significant Sikh population which has greatly enhanced our community. The Indian-Canadian community throughout Canada today is one of the communities that is very hard working, has a tremendous commitment to their families, to the community, to their religion, and to strengthening all of Canada.
But even now, today, in this House, I become perturbed when members of Parliament rise to present petitions that are deliberately aimed at preventing Sikhs and other minorities from joining the RCMP, because in order for them to join we might have to change a minor dress code to allow them to wear turbans as part of their religious faith. Sometimes I think we have come a long
September 27, 1989

way since 1914, and sometimes I wonder whether we have come very far at all.
I think we should look right now at some of the background of multiculturalism and the problems within our ethnic, multiracial and racial minorities in Canada. According to figures given by bureaucrats in the race relations sectors of Secretary of State, an attitudinal survey conducted in 1986 found that between 10 per cent and 15 per cent of Canadians were intolerant of visible minorities. Yet, at the same time, we know that between 1981 and 1986, 64 per cent of immigrants to this country were visible minorities. Fifty-four per cent of Canadians perceived an increase in racism. I think we have seen that in the last year in some of our metropolitan cities, particularly when we have problems like increased unemployment, problems of affordable housing, concerns that are expressed by many people about ethnic minorities and as immigration increases.
There is still systemic discrimination against visible minorities in employment. The government has set a low target of only 3.2 per cent for the hiring of visible minorities in the public service compared with an actual figure of 6.3 per cent in the work force. In actual percentages only 1.58 per cent were employed.
In language training and settlement programs, funding has been erratic. I shall be talking about that a little bit more. I want to talk about some of the weaknesses inherent in this act.
We are very quick to spout nice platitudes, but when it comes to putting in dollars to assist new immigrants to obtain some of the things that this bill sets out in terms of understanding the values inherent in Canadian citizenship and encouraging them to participate in the social, cultural, political, and economic life of Canada, the resources are not provided. Therefore I think we have to take a look at that.
Multicultural health care is now an issue. Governments and professionals are only beginning to recognize that different diets, lifestyles, and culture perspectives affect the type of illness a person may contract and the treatment they may opt for. Very little attention has
Government Orders
been paid to medical practice as it applies to other cultures.
There has been insensitivity shown by the media in covering causes that are overtly racist. In some of the programs that depict crimes, particularly in the city of Vancouver, the media has not brought attention to the fact that just as when I first started working in Vancouver in the social services in the late 1950s and early 1960s, there were worse gangs. They were not Oriental gangs. The problems with gangs in Vancouver is nothing new. They have nothing to do with immigration. They have to do with unemployment, dislocation of youth, poverty and lack of housing.
We have seen concerns being raised about the whole question of the notwithstanding clause as it might affect the rights of minorities, particularly as it might affect the rights of visible minorities. I think this is something we are going to have to take a look at in Canada. We feel that that clause, and where there are some reasons to continue with it, can be used by government to perpetuate injustice on minorities. We must remember that in the two incidents that I cited with the Sikhs and with the Japanese, it was the governments that were behind them with the support of the general public.
The New Democratic Party certainly supports this bill, but there are some shortcomings that I think must be addressed. One of the first shortcomings is that there is no increase in staff. There may be sharing of staff and facilities from Department of Secretary of State, especially in regional offices. That new department has serious responsibilities to monitor federal departments and institutions. Therefore, we anticipate that there is going to be a shortfall or insufficient staffing. It is very nice to have a bill, but if you do not provide the resources, it is not possible for a department to carry out its responsibilities.
This government has cut back on the Citizenship Instruction and Language Training programs. Since 1987, they have been reduced by 50 per cent. Now we understand that they are to be totally eliminated by 1990. Again, what is the purpose of having a department if you do not provide it with any resources? These Citizenship Instruction and Language Training programs are the backbone of getting new citizens integrated into Canadian society. That is the way you accomplish the goals that are set out in the act. To simply state goals is of very little value if you cannot, in fact, provide the resources. The bill says it is to provide "services for the acquisition and proof of citizenship". If you delete the ability and the resources to provide those services, what do you

Government Orders
have? You have a piece of paper. I think that is a weakness.
We are concerned still that there is not a commissioner or an ombudsperson as there is with official languages. We are delighted to see that the House leader for the government has today announced, mainly at the urging of my fellow New Democrat from Vancouver East, a separate standing committee on multiculturalism.
There is also a problem of overlapping with other areas, particularly in the area of immigrant women, that may allow departments to play games and may allow both this department and some of the other departments to take the "it's your problem" attitude, while at the same time neither of them providing the services and resources.
In summary, I would like to make two or three points. This is an important piece of legislation. It sets up a department that will have significance for the lives of most Canadians. It is worthy of support because at least it sets out some goals and some purposes. Unfortunately, we cannot be sure that those without resources are going to be enough. I think all Canadians have a vital stake in making Canadian multiculturalism work. Certainly, for people like myself, with my family background, it is vital.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member on his submissions, but he, along with the previous Conservative member who spoke seem to suggest that by passing an act to create a department of multiculturalism that somehow immigrants, new Canadians, will acquire new rights, that they will get something that they do not already have. That begs the question: does a policy of multiculturalism give to new Canadians and Canadians of ethnic origins something, or anything that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not give them? Surely the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that was passed by this House and embraced by this Parliament gives every Canadian, whether they were bom in Canada or elsewhere, similar rights. Therefore I think it is a mistake, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that this policy of multiculturalism and the
creation of a department of multiculturalism will somehow bestow new rights on certain Canadians.
The Conservative member who spoke said that it was intended to give new Canadians a special interest. Well, the simple answer to that is, no thanks. New Canadians, and the sons and daughters of immigrants, do not want special recognition. All they want is to be treated like every other Canadian.
The member talked about immigrants. Yes, special programs ought to be in place to ensure that new Canadians, immigrants to Canada, are assisted in their integration into Canadian life. But surely you do not need a policy of multiculturalism to achieve that. Surely that should be the responsibility of the Department of Immigration, the immigration policy of the Government of Canada, not only to establish the criteria for admission into Canada of new Canadians but also to assist them in their integration into Canada.
What this particular piece of legislation will do is this, and I think it is important to look at it in context. It will create a minister of multiculturalism, there will be a separate department of multiculturalism and then there will be a department of culture which again begs this question: What is the difference between Canadian culture and multiculturalism, and why would you need the two? Surely multiculturalism is part of Canadian culture.
I will put this question to the hon. member who just spoke: He was speaking about certain barriers that exist with respect to visible minorities in Canada. Does he not truly believe in his heart of hearts that this particular move by the government, rather than breaking down the barriers that exist in order to achieve full equality in Canada, will in effect create barriers in that it will distinguish Canadians based on their heritage? This is at a time when we ought to be promoting what we have in common. We ought not to be creating new barriers which will, in my view, exacerbate the already sensitive situation we have in Canada with respect to racial harmony.

The member feels that the introduction of this type of a department is a backward step. I cannot agree with him. I think that to focus within one ministry
September 27, 1989

the responsibility for citizenship and multiculturalism, including some of the other things that it is responsible for in terms of the promotion of race relations, is positive.
Canada is now going through another period where there is concern within the ethnic communities and particularly within the visible minorities. One of the things that I think Canada does that is different from some other countries that promote or accept large numbers of immigrants is that it values their diversity, it values their culture. We have undertaken not only to allow but to assist people from different nationalities to maintain their cultural identity.
The mosaic of Canada is, therefore, quite different from that of the United States where the intent there is to integrate and to play down any differences, to drop your background, your religion, your culture and your ethnicity when you become an American. Here in Canada I think we have done the opposite, much to the enrichment of our country.
Therefore, I think it is important to have a department that not only promotes multiculturalism and race relations but one which also ties them in with citizenship. What that basically says is that those are the things that go with being a Canadian citizen. I think that is where we have broken down in the past, in terms of our mistreatment or lack of equality for ethnic groups. What we have not done is say to the Japanese or to the Sikhs: "You have certain rights because you are a Canadian citizen and with that citizenship go these rights". I think that there is an importance in linking it within this type of ministry.
I would agree, however, with one thing that the member seems to be alluding to, that is, if there is not some substance and some resources provided then what we have is an empty shell. If what the government intends is to provide a department for window-dressing with no resources to carry out the goals that are stated in that bill, I will be the first one up on my feet to condemn it. If that is its intent, not only will the New Democratic Party but other Canadians very quickly see through it and condemn it.

Mr. Speaker, the member seemed to suggest that in order to acquire certain rights and freedoms, citizenship is a prerequisite. Just to correct the record, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not require citizenship as a prerequisite in order to be afforded the rights and privileges that attach to the
Government Orders
Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I want to make that absolutely clear. The Conservative members seem to be suggesting the same thing, that in order to have certain rights to equality and the right not to be discriminated against, Canadian citizenship is a prerequisite. In fact, it is deliberately not a prerequisite in that when parliamentarians decided on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, they specifically decided not to make it a prerequisite.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to participate today in this debate. It is an historic debate which establishes a new federal government department responsible for multiculturalism and citizenship.
These are important steps which flow from a landmark study done in 1960, the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism which is properly known as the Laurendeau-Danton report. It noted at that time in recognition of the diversity of the cultural groups found in Canada that "Canadian society, open and modem, should be able to integrate heterogeneous elements into a harmonious system to achieve unity in diversity".
I think much of the debate and differing points of view here relate to the fact that fundamentally, in adding this rich cultural diversity and recognizing it, we add to the fundamental characteristic which is in our constitution officially, the bilingual and bicultural nature of Canada. We are talking about the right for equal treatment and consideration under the laws of Canada.
I am very pleased because this government took an initiative that was started with Laurendeau-Danton in 1971 to establish a policy marking multiculturalism. This department becomes official through this act and I believe, if given adequate resources, can become a great symbol of the reality of our multicultural heritage and of the grandeur of our diverse ethnic mix, something that the people of Canada are becoming more and more aware of every day. We hope that this department can enrich the unique multicultural tapestry that is the Canadian society, enabling us to forge a new era of goodwill in the relationships among our people, notably respect, understanding and tolerance, which is the hallmark of Canadians with very few aberrant moments in our history.
As a new arm of the national government, this department should work to preserve and enhance the fundamental characteristics of Canada which I stated as being tolerant, open, peaceful and democratic. But let us not fool ourselves. The creation of this department is but

September 27, 1989
Government Orders
one step in the long process of integrating the ethnic, linguistic and multicultural aspects of our people with the day to day reality of life in this country. There is racism and those of us who do not care to acknowledge it move with a blind eye. If this department takes us one step toward the goal of eradicating that sense and undercurrent in society, we will have been successful with this move.
This department and this minister must be prepared to do battle against that growing undercurrent which I have talked about, and which I sense underneath this society. If we are to avoid major steps backward as a society, this trend must be stopped, and I hope this will be a major goal of the new department. If we are not more tolerant, then we fail the most democratic test of our modem society and of a modem democracy.
The challenge goes beyond institutions. I hope that this new department will be able to provide a leadership role so that its efforts, research and findings will become a guiding framework all across government and through this touch all aspects of Canadian life. The challenge is to direct our whole range of national programs toward integrating new Canadians and those who have been here for generations into all aspects of Canadian life in a coherent and proper manner.
It is not enough to support individual groups in society, visible minorities or others just in the enhancement of their own cultural expression. Song, dance and cultural festivals are important and serve to preserve individuality in society.
But we must, at the same time, seek integration through maximum participation in Canadian life. It should be considered a Canadian reality that a certain distinctiveness can be preserved while the process of integration is also put into practice. This is one role that I can see for this new department. Pursuing the dual objective: enhancement of cultural uniqueness coupled with a great emphasis on integration. The old maxim remains true: the whole of this country is far greater than the sum of its parts, as exciting and as rewarding as each of those parts can be.
The so-called politics of inclusion must be used here in Canada, not with the aim of forgetting the past, but integrating it into the present and the future as we build together a cohesive society able to address the challenges the next decades will bring.
I think this department, Mr. Speaker, should broaden our perspective. As we embark on establishing a new institution in this country it will gain its place around the cabinet table and in the political life of the country. We must use the opportunity to begin letting our cultural sensitivities pervade other aspects of government, of public discussion, and of our daily lives. Perhaps the visibility of this department will now ensure that education, job training, employment accessibility programs and law enforcement agencies all have a multicultural component to recognize differences, respect and reflect these differences, and see them as a positive aspect of our Canadian mosaic. And though perhaps a contradiction in terms, the creation of this new department may just help us meet our goal of seeing multiculturalism merged with all general cultural policies and thinking rather than being introduced and addressed in isolation.
Would it not be a wonderful irony if, by separating multiculturalism and citizenship off on their own, from a government perspective, it would achieve the goal of integrating them more from a human perspective, making them part and parcel of the Canadian way of thinking.
I said earlier that governments must go further than supporting multiculturalism through cultural expression, such as song, dance and folk festivals, and through other ministries and institutional fora. I believe that on the basis of mutual knowledge of cultures and opportunities to seek, establish and develop links, Canadians can be enriched by each other.
The view articulated in the charge to the 1984 Equality Now! committee task force, which was looking at the question of visible minorities in our Canadian society showed that while progress has been made, there are still many miles to go. I quote what was stated in the preamble: "Canada stands on the threshold of a new era. In a country with a long history of innovation, accommodation and tolerance, the challenge of an increasingly multicultural and multiracial society is one which can and should be met head on- The government must now
September 27, 1989

consciously choose a course of action which will ensure that there are no roadblocks preventing the full participation of all citizens in the cultural, social, economic and political life of this country".
Therefore, how is such enrichment to be achieved? There are many ways but time does not allow me to elaborate or be creative. However, let me suggest that we look at our law enforcement agencies and our employment-equity policies, they are the best places to start. I would also suggest one of the other ways that is all pervasive is the medium of broadcasting, television and radio, which are fundamentally a part of all of our lives and can serve the cause of strengthening sensitivities in the multilingual, multicultural racial areas of this country. Let us not forget that watching television is the number one leisure activity for Canadians. We spend more than 24 hours a week, on average, in front of the television set. Each year, Canadian children watch almost 1,000 hours of television compared to 800 hours spent in school.
As well, more than 50 per cent of Canadians say that radio and television is their principal source of news and information. That is the medium that can carry the message of who we are, what we are, and can reflect the exact colour, shape, dialogue and dialect that we use as Canadians.
I gave you these facts and figures because I believe it to be clear that Canadians of all races, all creeds, and all colours can find out what their society is like and what society thinks of them in part by the way they are portrayed through the media.
With the growth of television, media images have become a very important substitute for social integration. Therefore, we must ensure that broadcasting does not represent individuals and groups as a single North American type for we are not all the same and that must be recognized when we see ourselves on the screen.
Now Parliament has a golden opportunity with the imminent introduction of a new broadcasting bill to make sure that our broadcasting system through its programming is more reflective of the multicultural nature of Canada helping to meet the goals of society
Government Orders
and the objectives of the new department of multicultur-alism.
A new bill must not stop there. It must address, as I have said, employment equity and the absence of visible minorities in the media, not just on the screen but those behind the cameras, those on the media boards, the commissions and self-regulating bodies.
The government in its legislation must encourage the broadcasters in their hiring practices to be more reflective of the multicultural nature of Canadian society. This is just an example which could be extended to all phases of business activity in our country.
I would like to suggest that there are a few problems in this bill. My hon. colleague, the member for Saint-Laurent, pointed out that the definition section needs to clearly link this bill with Bill C-93, the Multiculturalism Act. There is a need for clarity as to who the minister really is, who will speak with the most force and authority at the cabinet table to bring to reality our vison of Canada for tomorrow.
The question has been raised by her as well about whether the bill adequately focuses on the separate areas sufficiently, that is, the area of responsibility for citizenship separate from that of multiculturalism. There must be a distinct description of the responsibilities in each of these areas.
I would hope that in legislative committee partisan politics will not be played out in this very sensitive area of our Canadian vision for a Canadian way of life, and that thoughtful amendments from any side of this House to improve the operative sections of the bill will be warmly appreciated and the needed changes made.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I bring to your attention that the United Nations has proclaimed this period, 1987 to 1997, the world decade for cultural development. One of the objectives of this decade is the international recognition of equal dignity for and of all cultures. It is my hope that within Canada we could achieve this objective.
I think we can be a role model for the nations of the world. We must be confident that we can become more accepting, more aware of the true value of our diversity, but also realize how fortunate we are to be so diverse in the first place.

September 27, 1989
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the member on her speech. I have had an opportunity over the last five years to work with her .1 want to say that in those five years I have enjoyed the opportunity of working on a very special committee of the Equality Rights Committee that reported to the Parliament of Canada in the form of a report called Equality For All.
I know that her comments come from a position of knowledge of the importance of this issue of citizenship and multiculturalism, the pluralistic aspect of this bill that is so important at this time in our history.
I want to say that I was pleased to see her emphasize in her comments the importance of tolerance in our communities. Every once in a while this issue of racism raises its head and I think we are all outraged with it. Her comments on tolerance were so very important and well taken today, as well as the understanding that we must have between the various communities.
I would like to ask the member what her advice would be to other colleagues in her Party who oppose this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to address the member for Scarborough. I have very pleasant memories of the almost year we spent together on a daily schedule which was rather rugged travelling across this land. I see one of her other colleagues is the Associate Minister of National Defence. Certainly, the area of defence was one to which we paid a great deal of attention.

The misogynists are there in force.

Equality now, equality for all; respect, tolerance and understanding, and you asked me about differences of points of view. That is one of the great qualities of Canadians. All Canadians, hopefully on your side or my side of this house, are open, tolerant and understanding of differences. This difference that you are alluding to is perhaps a difference of time line. It is my hope that in
the future we will not need to have a committee, department, minister or bill to address multiculturalism per se. I hope it will disappear in terms of its need over time. I would eventually agree with the member's colleague sitting behind you that we will eventually have the department of Canadianism or the department of culture. However, we have not reached that stage yet. I think I mentioned there is this ongoing need to recognize that there is racism just below the skin and we really must address it.
It is an unfortunate reality that we have not built a system of integration into the Canadian way of life as we receive and absorb new immigrants. I would hope that the minister will find a way to improve the integration and acceptance of new Canadians, and find mechanisms within our law enforcement agencies. In my city the level of racism between the various visible minority groups is of great concern. There have been some unfortunate incidents of late which only underscore the need to work at many levels in our society to reach nirvana, that point in the history of development of Canada where we will not need multiculturalism. In that regard, I would say that he is perhaps 10 steps ahead of where we are right now. Let us hope that we reach where he is some day.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to make a comment, since as you probably all know, I was very busy with the election campaign which has just ended in Quebec. I took part in the campaign as a Liberal militant. I worked very hard for Liberal candidates and I offer no apologies for the fact. Certainly not! I am very proud of the fact.
During the campaign, some very unfortunate comments were made about the majority in Quebec by a new party which calls itself the Equality Party. Strange that a party called the Equality Party would, through its founding president, practically spit in the face of those of us people in Quebec who try to explain what it means for a people to survive. I just couldn't why. Perhaps some day here in the House we could have a debate in which we could express the feelings of the majority in Quebec that sees its numbers dwindling at an incredible rate because of the low birth rate and an aging population.
September 27, 1989

If this bill could bring us to a better understanding of what racism is, perhaps some of the unfortunate statements we heard in Quebec, references to fascists and nazis and comparisons of the Quebec situation with what is going on in South Africa, in that case I believe this bill will have been tremendously useful. I say this, and I am sorry that I have to say it, and I hope, in the weeks and months to come, that here in the House we will reflect and draw the necessary conclusions before we make a final decision about other political events that are expected to take place next June, and I am not referring to the leadership of the Liberal Party of Canada, I am referring to Meech Lake. So I hope we will have a chance to get back to this question.
I also hope we will have a chance to explain how, when people speak without thinking, and this also applies to the people who made those unfortunate statements, whoever they happen to be, and I am not naming names- I don't want to get into particulars, because today I especially wanted to say how happy I was to be able to take part in this campaign. If you really want to know the issues, an election campaign is the place to be. I also want to congratulate those who were elected and who are not of the same political stripe as we are. We cannot blame people for voting for a party that calls itself the Equality Party. After all, this is a democracy. In fact, I am almost glad this party exists, because as a result, the party for which I worked may move to the centre between two extremes, which should improve our relations in the future.
But if this particular bill, and here I agree with the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), could help us to fight all forms of racism-but when we talk about fighting all forms of racism, we must not be selective. It's like when we fight for human rights, we don't have the right to be selective. We either believe in human rights or we don't. We can't pick and choose. We can't select some people rather than others because they are more important, better organized, richer, and ignore the destitute. Either we believe in this principle or we don't. Either we fight racism or we don't.
And that is why, without being directly involved today in the debate on second reading of this bill, I nevertheless intend to take a close look at the legislation, Mr. Speaker, and to become actively involved, because I have a lot to say about the development of multiculturalism in Canada. I believe that together, we can make this a
Government Orders
better bill, as long as the Government doesn't insist on believing that the bill is perfect. There have been a number of developments since multiculturalism was first introduced under Mr. Trudeau. A lot has happened and much experience has been gained.
I listened to what was said by the Hon. Member from Toronto, and I must say it made me think. I feel I ought to give due consideration to what the Hon. Member,for whom I have a great deal of respect, had to say. He may belong to a minority group, he may feel like a minority, but as you know, minorities are not always wrong.
The Hon. Member asked us to think carefully before we pass this bill, and I want to thank him for that. I also wish to thank my other colleague who reminded us that we should have an absolute horror of racism in all its forms. I hope that in future elections, people will be more careful and refrain from distasteful comments of this kind, especially when addressed to an entire population. I realize no one is absolutely blameless, but we cannot attack a group as such just because we don't like them.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that I share my colleague's view and hope for the eradication of racism and bigotry and that sane heads and careful language will guide our direction, wherever we are in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that we do not have a better system to tell Members who are speaking how much time they have taken and especially how much time they have left to speak.
I recognize the difficulty, because in the heat of action, it is not always easy for us to think about time constraints.

But I think that we will have to improve the system the House uses to control the time allowed. Otherwise the Chair has trouble knowing whether it is 10 minutes, 5 or 20.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to offer my contribution to the debate on Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
The Bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, is about what makes Canada special.
Last year in the House we considered the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, and as a Parliament consisting of people speaking both official languages and coming from the four comers of this country, we endorsed this very important aspect of our Canadian identity.
The department will play a major role during this last decade of the twentieth century. At its core lies our constitutional commitment to two official languages, and our recognition of our cultural and racial diversity. The department has three crucial missions.
The first consists in further consolidating our unique position among the nations of the American continent. To a large extent, this position derives from our recognition of two official languages and the store we set by the various cultures of all Canadians.
This position also derives from the means we have chosen to reflect these realities and respect them.
Although it would be misrepresentation of the facts that we have always lived in harmony, our history proves that as Canadians we have a special aptitude for compromise, for seeking reasonable solutions and for acting as mediators in case of conflict.
These aptitudes, together with the flexibility of our institutions, are so many characteristics that are the envy of other nations. It is characteristics like these that are judged essential in a world that demands an increasing ability to adapt to change.
The department's second mission is to ensure that no one in our society is deprived of the ability to participate in that society as a result of constraints such as illiteracy or cultural or racial background.
In cases where our society has been unable to give its citizens a satisfactory level of proficiency in reading, writing and arithmetic, we have failed. Where our society perpetuates discrimination in any form, including discrimination based on the misconception that a particular race or group of persons is superior to others, we have failed. We cannot claim to be that generous and compassionate society we aspire to be, as long as this kind of situation is allowed to exist.
The third mission of the department is to create a climate and conditions which will enable all Canadians to contribute to building our future. By pooling the various assets of our fellow citizens we have at our disposal the combined knowledge, experience and wisdom of all the world's cultures. This is a tremendous wealth which is our very own. It is a wealth which must be put to good use if we want to face up to the challenges that can be expected in the near future. It is a wealth which is
September 27, 1989

absolutely essential to the fulfilment of our promising future.
Mr. Speaker, this department will not be a regulating or controling agency. It will not attempt to maintain the statu quo, nor will it be chained to the past. It will look to the future and actively seek to eliminate whatever obstacles might limit our aspirations. Its mission will be to convince us, make us aware of the reality, throw us challenges, and urge us to become simple society which will grow and command the respect of all nations the world over.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill under study is the logical continuation of the work done by the House last year, but as my Quebec colleague said, the Secretary of State and Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship (Mr. Weiner), it is much more than simple legislation to establish a federal department. As I see it, a department such as we want to establish today deals with the many issues and values we all share. I am convinced that the object of the Bill is more than a mere consolidation of Government programs. It conveys the vision

strong Canada looking to the future. That is why I am proud to take part in this debate.
The existence of a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will be significant for the people of Montreal, Moncton, Trois-Rivieres, as well as Toronto, Winnipeg and Saskatoon. It will be just as significant for Quebecers as it will be for all other Canadians' groups, for our native people as for our citizens whose forefathers came here with Champlain or with the Loyalists.
Mr. Speaker, we are debating a bill to establish a new Department. This bill follows a commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), on September 25, 1988, confirmed on election night, and reiterated in the Speach from the Throne.
Mr. Speaker, in studying this bill, we will realize its importance for all Canadians. With this bill, we will bring Canadians closer together, and establish a government agency mandated to encourage our people to build a stronger Canada for the future.
